candidates.title: Sound Lantern
candidates.pitch: A lantern that shines sound: a beam sweeps around the player like a lighthouse while walls hum and every passage mouth rings a chime whose pitch tells how deep it runs, and one input (space, tap, gamepad button or an assistive switch) commits to the passage the beam is crossing. Each sweep is a small gamble, because another full revolution gives better information while the flood rises, and the whole cave plays with the screen dark, or by radar and captions alone for players who cannot hear. Afterwards the cave is revealed as a map with the player's ribbon route beside the best route.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless as a design, with a seasonal nudge: October 15 is White Cane Safety Day in the US (as of 2026-10-11, per Paths to Literacy and Mass.gov). The page is framed as an audio game made for everyone, not as a simulation of blindness.

research.summary: Click echolocation is documented by independent research groups (blind experts, and sighted novices after training), so reading a space by ear is a real skill. Audio-only games with binaural 3D sound exist (an audio-only iPhone title; student and thesis projects for visually impaired players) and sighted players enjoy them too. Switch scanning, where an indicator advances on its own and one switch selects, is the standard single-input method in assistive technology, and the Game Accessibility Guidelines favor very simple control schemes for switch users. The precedence effect fuses echoes within a few to tens of ms, so the page codes distance by pitch and chimes instead of tiny delays. The secretary problem (the 37 percent rule) frames the sweep dilemma. Critiques from blind advocates of blindfold-style simulations shape the framing: an audio game, not a simulation.

sources.title: Depth Echolocation Learnt by Novice Sighted People
sources.snippet: PLOS ONE paper on sighted novices learning to judge depth from click echoes. The search summary says novices improved, which suggests total loss of sight is not required.
sources.note: Sighted novices can learn click-based depth echolocation. Not opened; the summary was blended, but the title carries the finding and two other papers agree.

sources.title: Human click-based echolocation: Effects of blindness and age, and real-life implications in a 10-week training program
sources.snippet: A 10-week training study. Per the search summary, both sighted and blind participants improved considerably and neither age nor blindness limited learning speed.
sources.note: A second research group reports trainable click echolocation in sighted and blind adults.

sources.snippet: Analysis of mouth clicks recorded from blind expert echolocators, with a model for synthesizing them. Numeric click properties came only from a blended summary and are not relied on.
sources.note: Blind experts echolocate with self-made mouth clicks; the click timing and beam-width figures stay unverified and are not used on the page.

sources.title: Precedence effect
sources.snippet: Encyclopedia entry. Per the search summary, similar sounds close in time fuse into one event; fusion holds for about 1 to 5 ms for clicks and up to about 40 ms for complex sounds.
sources.note: Why distance is coded by pitch and chimes rather than by realistic millisecond echo delays.

sources.title: What is Haas Effect and how to take advantage of it
sources.snippet: An audio-equipment company blog; the search summary attributes to it a fusion limit of up to about 50 ms for complex sounds and about 100 ms for music.
sources.note: Second independent source for the fusion window; figures differ by source and by stimulus.

sources.title: Secretary problem
sources.snippet: Encyclopedia entry on optimal stopping. Per the search summary, rejecting about the first n/e candidates and then taking the next best-so-far wins with probability near 1/e, about 37 percent.
sources.note: Frames the commit-or-resweep dilemma. The game allows recall at a cost, so the classic result is an analogy, not the exact optimum of the game.

facts.claim: Several independent research groups report that people, blind experts and sighted novices after training, can judge distance or position from the echoes of their own mouth clicks (PLOS ONE and PLOS Computational Biology papers seen in search results).

Audio-first games built on binaural or 3D directional sound exist: Papa Sangre is an audio-only iPhone game whose levels are navigated by sound alone, and academic projects (Connecticut College, UMass Dartmouth) built audio games for visually impaired players.
Switch access scanning advances an indicator through items on its own, by highlight or by voice, and the user selects the current item by activating a single switch.

As of 2026-10-11, per the Game Accessibility Guidelines, a guideline recommends very simple control schemes compatible with switch or eye-tracking devices, with a one-button endless runner as the example (reported by one organization, unverified).

In the precedence effect, similar sounds close together in time are heard as one event; the fusion window is roughly 1 to 5 ms for clicks and tens of ms (about 30 to 50) for complex sounds, beyond which a separate echo is heard.
In the secretary problem, rejecting roughly the first n/e (about 37 percent) of candidates and then taking the first one better than all seen so far succeeds with probability near 1/e.

Blind advocates and researchers criticize blindfold-style disability simulations; a review hosted by the National Federation of the Blind reports they can lower how capable blind people are judged to be, and design writers raise similar objections.
White Cane Safety Day is observed in the US on October 15, and October is marked as White Cane Awareness Month by Massachusetts.

design.coreLoop: At each chamber a beam of sound orbits the player once every few seconds (adjustable). A tick marks straight ahead, a continuous hum carries wall distance (nearer is brighter and louder), and each passage mouth rings a chime whose pitch encodes how far the passage runs, with wind layered on the exit direction and flutter on hazards. A single input commits to the passage under the beam at that instant (nearest mouth wins within an adjustable tolerance); a press between mouths bonks and costs a revolution. The player then walks the passage by footstep sound to the next chamber. A flood clock rises with every revolution, so each sweep poses an optimal-stopping choice between committing on partial information and paying for another full revolution. The run ends at the exit with a reveal map: the cave, the player's ribbon route, and the solver's best route. Daily seeds and hash-shared caves keep the second and tenth run different.
sophisticationHooks: One deterministic percept stream, four renderers: a pure core turns each sweep into timed events (hum curve, tick, chimes, wind, flutter), consumed by a WebAudio renderer (AudioParam value curves and scheduled oscillators on the audio clock), a canvas radar, an aria-live caption feed, and optional vibration, so hearing, sight and touch are equal ways to play.

Cave engine: seeded Poisson-disc chambers, a minimum spanning tree plus extra loops under a planarity check, zigzag passage ribbons, a union signed-distance field, 96 to 128 ray-marched samples per sweep with hysteresis opening detection, and Dijkstra over walking time plus sweeps for par; decoy alcoves are placed so a greedy deepest-chime policy sometimes fails.

Input timing core: the beam angle is a pure function of audio-clock time; a press maps through a latency offset from tap-along calibration, then through assist tolerance and snap-to-nearest-mouth, with revolution period and tolerance adjustable so players with slower or less precise input run at their own pace.

Hearing-robust coding: direction rides on stereo pan, on time since the tick, and on the chime pitch contour at once, so mono speakers, one-ear listening and different hearing profiles still work; a setup step sets the volume ceiling and pitch range behind a limiter.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: cave generator and solver (about 350 lines), sweep sampler and percept events (about 250), WebAudio renderer with six voices (hum, tick, chime, wind, flutter or drip, footstep) (about 300), canvas radar and reveal map (about 250), UI shell with settings (speed, tolerance, mono, captions, contrast, reduced motion, lights-out), about and making-of panel, daily seed with URL-hash sharing, localStorage bests. Cut if short: collectible moths, moving bats, biome variety, free-steer mode, spoken direction labels, vibration.
risks: Builders and QA cannot hear the result; mitigation: every mapping is a pure function with checkable outputs, captions mirror each percept in the DOM for inspection, and a built-in audio test strip plays each voice.
Disability-simulation critique (blind advocates, design writers): the copy presents an audio game for everyone and makes no empathy or blindfold claims; the about panel credits audio-game precedents.

Autoplay and mobile audio quirks: sound starts only after a gesture, resumes after tab changes, and the game pauses when hidden. Timing jitter and output latency vary by device; audio-clock timing plus calibration handle it, but headless QA cannot test it.
Loudness and hearing safety: a compressor, a volume ceiling and a setup step come before any sound plays.
Distance is coded by pitch and chimes, not realistic echo delays, because the precedence effect fuses short delays; the about panel says the acoustics are stylized.

Unverified: the Game Accessibility Guidelines wording (one organization) and the Web Audio panner details (MDN only). Fallbacks are a plain StereoPannerNode plus pitch coding, and the page shows the guideline as 'as of 2026-10-11, per Game Accessibility Guidelines'.

candidates.title: Eyes Only
candidates.pitch: Each plate is a mosaic of colored dots hiding a creature or a letter, and each of five simulated eyes (typical, protan, deutan, tritan, achromat) reads a different part of the picture. The visitor flips lenses, with a severity dial for milder forms, to see what each eye reveals, decodes cipher words whose letters need different eyes, and builds plates in a studio where a solver tunes the dots until exactly the chosen eyes can read them. A real lab result, dichromats out-spotting trichromats on color-camouflaged texture, inspires the masked plates, so the eye most often called deficient is the one that cracks the code.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. About 1 in 12 men have a color vision deficiency (as of 2026-10-11, per NEI), and the science behind the plates (camouflage-breaking studies, a 2009 simulation model) is stable and citable.

research.summary: A 1992 study reported that dichromats beat trichromats at finding texture-defined targets hidden by random red-green coloring, and a later review states dichromats do better when color is irrelevant to the task; early stimuli were stylized, so the effect is real but task-dependent. A 2009 IEEE TVCG paper by Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes gives a physiologically based simulation model covering dichromacy and anomalous trichromacy. About 1 in 12 men have a color vision deficiency (NEI), and deuteranomaly, a milder form, is the most common type, which motivates a severity dial. A cone-opponent view (luminance, red-green, blue-yellow) explains what each lens keeps; one paper cautions that some dichromats keep residual red-green discrimination. The design splits plates into exact ones (pure channel signals that vanish after the lens by construction) and perceptual ones (masking, labeled as a model).

sources.title: Dichromats detect colour-camouflaged objects that are not detected by trichromats
sources.snippet: PubMed record of Morgan, Adam and Mollon (Proc. R. Soc. B). Per the search summary, random red-green coloring of texture elements made the target harder for trichromats but not for dichromats, who did better.
sources.note: The core finding that inspires the masked plates. Not opened; the title states the finding and a later review agrees. Year 1992 comes from the search summary.

sources.title: Relative advantages of dichromatic and trichromatic color vision in camouflage breaking
sources.snippet: Review article. The search summary says it reports dichromats outperforming trichromats at finding camouflaged targets when color is irrelevant to the task, and that early stimuli were stylized shapes with extreme colors.
sources.note: Independent review supporting the finding and its limits (stylized stimuli); the limit goes into the risks.

sources.title: A physiologically-based model for simulation of color vision deficiency
sources.snippet: University repository record of the Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes paper (IEEE TVCG 15(6), 1291-1298). Per the abstract in the search summary, one model handles normal vision, anomalous trichromacy and dichromacy.
sources.note: The simulation model behind the lens engine. The abstract was seen only through a search summary.

sources.title: Color Blindness
sources.snippet: National Eye Institute overview page. Per the search summary, its fact box says about 1 in 12 men have color vision deficiency, and women are less often affected because the common genes are X-linked.
sources.note: Headline prevalence, attributed explicitly to NEI in the summary. Not opened.

sources.title: About Colour Blindness - Colour Blind Awareness
sources.snippet: Colour Blind Awareness page. Per the search summary, sources commonly give about 1 in 12 men (8 percent) and 1 in 200 women; that summary blended several results.
sources.note: Second organization for the prevalence figure (blended summary, but the title matches the topic).

sources.title: Types of Color Vision Deficiency - National Eye Institute - NIH
sources.snippet: NEI page grouping deuteranomaly (the most common red-green type), protanomaly, protanopia and deuteranopia; blue-yellow forms are less common and complete color blindness is rare.
sources.note: Names the lens types and shows that milder anomalous forms dominate, which motivates the severity dial.

sources.title: The evolution of concepts of color vision - PMC
sources.snippet: Review. The search summary says only a fraction of color-defective males are true dichromats (roughly 1 percent protanopes and 2 percent deuteranopes) and partial forms are much more common.
sources.note: Independent review agreeing that milder forms dominate.

sources.title: Curing Color Blindness-Mice and Nonhuman Primates - PMC
sources.snippet: Review. Per the search summary, dichromats keep blue-yellow and black-white percepts and achromatic channels that carry brightness, but lack the normal sensations of red and green.
sources.note: Supports the lens-channel model: luminance and blue-yellow survive for red-green dichromats.

sources.title: Why do Protan & Deutan look so similar?
sources.snippet: Blog post. Per the search summary, luminance is the sum of the cone signals and the red-green channel compares red and green cone signals, so losing either cone type removes the red-green channel.
sources.note: Secondary explanatory source agreeing with the review on the channel structure; a blog, so weighted lightly.

sources.title: escholarship.org (UC eScholarship PDF; result title shown as 'escholarship.org')
sources.snippet: Per the search summary, a paper reports protanopes and deuteranopes are believed unable to make small-field red-versus-green judgments but argues some residual red-green discrimination may exist.
sources.note: Single-source caveat that the complete-loss view is contested; kept as a risk, not as a page fact.

facts.claim: Morgan, Adam and Mollon (Proc. R. Soc. B, 1992) reported that dichromats detected color-camouflaged texture targets that trichromats found harder, because random color interferes with texture-based segregation; a later review reports dichromats outperform trichromats when color is irrelevant to the task.

Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes published a physiologically based color vision deficiency simulation model in IEEE TVCG 15(6), 1291-1298 (2009); the abstract, seen through a search summary, says it covers normal vision, anomalous trichromacy and dichromacy.
About 1 in 12 men have a color vision deficiency, and women are far less often affected (NEI; Colour Blind Awareness).
Deuteranomaly, a milder anomalous form of red-green deficiency, is the most common type, and partial forms are more common than true dichromacy.
Red-green dichromats lose the red-green opponent signal but keep luminance (achromatic) and blue-yellow signals.
As of 2026-10-11, per a UC eScholarship paper (one source, unverified), some protanopes and deuteranopes may keep residual red-green discrimination, so a channel model is a simplification.

design.coreLoop: A seeded plate packs about two thousand dots of mixed radii; a hidden figure is encoded as a small offset in chosen cone-contrast directions (L, M, S or luminance) with masking noise in others. The visitor switches among five lenses (keys 1 to 5) or drags a severity dial, moves a reticle to the figure, and receives a per-lens detectability readout plus a reveal card explaining which eyes could read the plate and why. Cipher mode spreads a word over plates, one letter per subset of eyes. Studio mode takes a target set of readers and runs a solver that tunes channel amplitudes and noise until the model's detectability meets the target, or reports the target infeasible. A map of all 32 reader subsets fills in as plates are made, with unreachable cells greyed out, which gives a collection goal for the tenth minute.
sophisticationHooks: Lens engine: 3x3 linear-RGB simulation matrices in the Machado style with a severity dial from typical to full dichromacy (anomalous trichromacy included), an achromat luminance lens, and self-tests (neutral gray unchanged; red-green pairs collapse under deutan and protan; blue-yellow pairs collapse under tritan).

Plate generator: seeded blue-noise circle packing with mixed radii on a spatial hash grid, figure masks from signed-distance creature shapes and a 5x7 glyph set, dot colors sampled in a cone-contrast space with gamut-safe scaling, fully deterministic from the URL hash.

Detectability model: a d-prime style score per lens (figure versus ground difference over pooled noise in the channels the lens still has) plus a clutter term where chromatic noise masks luminance signals for lenses that still see it, the Morgan-style effect; exact plates (pure channel signals) are separated from perceptual plates (masking) and labeled.

Studio solver and feasibility map: coordinate-descent search with restarts over signal mix, amplitude and per-channel noise to hit any of the 32 reader subsets; subsets that violate the channel structure are shown infeasible under the model and greyed in the map.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: lens engine and self-tests (about 250 lines), generator and renderer (about 300), detectability model and solver (about 250), UI for Hunt, Cipher and Studio modes with keyboard reticle and touch, severity dial, reveal cards, 12 specimen shapes and the glyph set, 40 curated seeds, URL-hash sharing, about and making-of panel listing verified sources only. Cut if short: sonified plate (pitch from local detectability), image import, palette tool, per-lens custom mixing.
risks: Perceptual claims: whether a typical eye misses a masked plate depends on the person and the display; the page grades by the model and labels those plates perceptual, while exact plates are true by construction.
The page is a puzzle and a model, not a vision test or diagnosis; the copy avoids telling any visitor what their own vision is.

Simulation caveats: disability-simulation critiques, residual red-green discrimination reported for some dichromats (one source, unverified), and varied displays; the about panel states them and shows the residual-discrimination point as 'as of 2026-10-11, per UC eScholarship'.

The camouflage advantage is documented for stylized stimuli and specific tasks (per a review in the search results), so the copy states it as a lab result and makes no general claim about colorblind people.
Matrix constants have to be reproduced from the published model without opening it; the fallback derives lenses from an LMS projection and the self-tests check neutrals and confusion-pair collapse.
A visual puzzle is not fully playable by blind visitors; text reveal cards and the optional sonified plate (cut if short) are the mitigation.
